title: The Natural History of Bone Stress Injuries in Athletes: From Inception to Resolution
claims: Bone stress injuries have been reported to account for 15% to 20% of all musculoskeletal injuries in cross-country, track and field, triathlon, duathlon and recreational running athletes.
Most bone stress injuries in endurance runners occur in the lower limb (80% to 95%), mainly in the tibia (49%) and tarsal bones (25%).
Female runners have a bone stress injury incidence 1.8 to 2.3 times higher than male runners, and female triathletes have a 2.9-fold higher rate than male triathletes.
In an Australian high-performance audit covering 48 sports over three years, 66% of bone stress injuries occurred during training and 7% during competition.

Recurrence is common: one study reported that 15% of athletes across sports had two or more bone stress injuries during a three-year surveillance period, and lumbar spine recurrence in cricket was 39%.

Risk factors for bone stress injury include female sex, competitive participation, problematic low energy availability, vitamin D or iron deficiency, irregular menstrual cycles and training prescription errors.
Some studies report increased bone stress injury risk in female adolescent athletes training 12 to 16 hours or more per week and in male adolescents running more than 30 miles a week.
